title: Constructive Algorithms
relevance: High — Div2 B/C (often D) constantly ask “build any valid array/string/graph/ops”; OAs rephrase the same as “return one feasible configuration / -1”.
company_notes: OA/interview variants: return any length-n array with sum S and no subarray/subset equal to X (Game With Array / Make Good); rearrange/rebuild a binary string under run or transition constraints (Team / Binary String Constructing, common phone-screen); assign blocks to k workers with load gap ≤x (Phoenix and Towers — greedy to current minimum); output ops that transform/sort under a weird op with a proven O(n) bound (Replace by MEX / Fence Painting).

phases.goal: Establish that the task is to output any valid object (or -1), not only a yes/no decision.

must_hit.point: Constructive problems require outputting an object (array, permutation, string, coloring, edge labels, or operation list) that meets the constraints, not merely deciding YES/NO.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says they must build/print one feasible configuration, not just check existence.

must_hit.point: Recognize the pattern from phrasing like “construct any”, “print one example”, “find a sequence of ≤K ops”, or “impossible → -1”.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps those stems to constructive output (and -1 when impossible).

must_hit.point: OA rephrasings of the same skill ask to return one feasible configuration or -1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions OA-style “return any valid array/string/ops or -1” as the same pattern.

probes: How do you tell this is constructive rather than a pure decision problem?
What output does the judge actually accept when multiple answers are valid?

hints.1: Look at whether the statement asks you to print an object or only YES/NO.
hints.2: Scan for “construct any”, “print one example”, ops under a bound, or impossible → -1.
hints.3: You must output an array/string/graph/ops (or -1); any valid object is enough.

phases.goal: Lock the workflow: existence condition, then simplest parametric construction, then edge-case casework.

must_hit.point: Write the NO/-1 existence condition first (parity, sum bounds, degree, count of 1s even, n small) before inventing the object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states impossibility checks before describing how to build the answer.

must_hit.point: Prefer a simple parametric family: periods, powers of two, all-1s + one big, SPF/prime labels, checkerboard, zigzag columns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names a fixed simple family instead of searching for a minimal or exotic object.

must_hit.point: Most Div2 constructive splits into 2–4 cases (n mod k / parity / has a high-degree vertex?), each with a fixed pattern.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Plans short casework with one canned pattern per case.

probes: What do you check before you start constructing?
If many objects work, what kind of answer family do you reach for first?

hints.1: Don’t build first—decide when the answer is impossible.
hints.2: Workflow: existence → simplest family → hand-check edge cases.
hints.3: NO/-1 from parity/sum/degree/even count of 1s/small n; then periods, powers of two, checkerboard, SPF, or greedy heap.

phases.goal: Show concrete construction templates used on Div2/OA constructive staples.

must_hit.point: Binary/run constructions: place the scarcer bit for exact transitions, or place the majority bit in blocks then inject the other (impossible-case first).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes block/scarce-bit placement and states impossibility before building.

must_hit.point: Load/segment constructions: always put the next block on the current shortest tower (heap), or fill zeros via a max-heap of longest-mid segments.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions greedy-to-minimum heap or longest-segment priority heap.

must_hit.point: Invariant tricks: append ≤3 numbers so sum = 2·xor (Make Good), or build Game With Array as S−n+1 then 1s with YES iff S odd or S ≥ 2n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls the XOR/sum append construction and/or the one-big-plus-ones array with that YES condition.

must_hit.point: Graph/tree defaults: extreme labels on a star/centroid/degree-≥3 vertex; paths and bipartite 2-colorings; e.g. alternate 2 and 3 on a path, or put 0,1,2 on three edges of a degree-≥3 vertex.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses path/bipartite toolkit or concentrates special labels on a high-degree/centroid vertex.

probes: Walk through one explicit construction you’d emit for a “any valid array” OA.
How would you assign blocks to m towers with height difference capped?

hints.1: Pick a fixed pattern, not a search.
hints.2: Think heap-on-shortest, SPF labels, checkerboard, or path prime alternation.
hints.3: Example templates: S−n+1 plus 1s; ≤3 append for sum=2·xor; heap to current shortest tower; 0,1,2 on a degree-≥3 vertex’s edges.

phases.goal: Treat loose operation/length bounds as permission for a simple correct construction with a proven op count.

must_hit.point: Do not minimize unless asked; loose length/ops bounds such as ≤2n or ≤1e4 invite a dumb correct construction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says any feasible object under the given bound is enough—no optimization chase.

must_hit.point: For operation constructions, prove an upper bound on ops, then emit a sequence that always stays under it (Prefix-Flip / MEX-sort / centroid-move style).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States a bound first, then describes a procedure guaranteed to respect it.

must_hit.point: OA operation-list constructive often targets a proven O(n) bound (Replace by MEX / Fence Painting style).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions building an explicit op list with an O(n)-style guarantee.

probes: The statement allows ≤2n operations—how does that change your construction?
What do you prove before you start emitting the operation list?

hints.1: Loose caps are not a request to minimize.
hints.2: Prove an ops upper bound, then implement a sequence under it.
hints.3: Use a simple construction that stays within ≤2n / ≤1e4 (or an O(n) op list), not the shortest possible.

phases.goal: Catch the usual constructive failure modes: skipped impossibility, over-optimizing, and missed edge cases.

must_hit.point: Skipping the existence/NO/-1 check and inventing an object that fails parity, sum bounds, degree, even count of 1s, or small-n cases.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that many WA come from building when the answer should be impossible.

must_hit.point: Trying to minimize length/ops or search for a clever object when the judge accepts any valid answer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says they would ship a simple parametric answer unless minimization is required.

must_hit.point: Constructive bugs are almost always missed edge cases—debug with a local checker for small n (brute all outputs vs your pattern).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Proposes validating the pattern on small n against a brute checker.

probes: Where do constructive submissions usually WA?
When is minimizing the construction the wrong instinct?

hints.1: Think about what you forgot to rule out before building.
hints.2: Existence first; don’t minimize; hand-check edge cases.
hints.3: Write NO/-1 conditions up front; ship any valid simple family; brute-check small n for missed cases.

tradeoffs.topic: Any valid object vs minimized object
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Unless asked to minimize, prefer the simplest parametric family under the stated length/ops bound (≤2n, ≤1e4, etc.); optimizing wastes time and adds edge-case risk.

tradeoffs.topic: Shape a fixed pattern vs search
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Shape the answer with a canned pattern (zigzag columns, checkerboard, SPF labels, greedy heap) rather than searching; Labs-style “shape the matrix, don’t search”.

tradeoffs.topic: Existence casework vs one universal formula
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Most Div2 constructive work is 2–4 cases (parity / n mod k / high-degree vertex) each with a fixed pattern, not one formula that covers every n.

gotchas.trap: Building the object before writing the impossibility condition.
gotchas.correction: Existence first: parity, sum bounds, degree, even count of 1s, small n → print NO/-1, then construct.

gotchas.trap: Overfitting to a minimal or “clever” answer when any feasible object works.
gotchas.correction: Judge accepts any valid object; use periods, powers of two, all-1s + one big, checkerboard, SPF, or greedy-to-shortest.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a construction that works for large n also covers tiny n or pure special counts.
gotchas.correction: Casework on small n and pure cases (e.g. impossible for n≤3 on Special Permutation; handle pure n1 in Binary String Reconstruction); verify with a small-n checker.

gotchas.trap: For tree/edge-label tasks, labeling arbitrarily instead of concentrating extremes.
gotchas.correction: Default toolkit: paths, bipartite 2-colorings, and extreme labels on a star/centroid/degree-≥3 vertex (e.g. 0,1,2 on three edges; alternate 2 and 3 on a path).
